_source: MS Forms result screenshots, questions 1-22, transcribed 1 Oct 2026. Form ID 1 (researcher's test submission) removed.
_scale: Part A: 1 = not at all ... 5 = extremely

A7_missing.R02: Operational reliability/operability: pipeline success rate, freshness-SLA; secondarily skills/talent availability (time-to-hire for the stack).
A7_missing.R04: Reliability, resilience and operational robustness. I would measure it through availability/SLA, failure recovery time, recovery point/time objectives, incident frequency and the operational effort required to maintain reliable data pipelines and products.
A7_missing.R05: What's missing is the role of the service-provider partnership. Solution architects are typically constrained by the toolset their platform partner offers — Google, Amazon, or Databricks — so the shape of any solution is largely determined by who the company chooses to partner with.
A7_missing.R06: You have two architecture options. Which improvement would matter more to your decision: A) a 30% lower three-year TCO, or B) a 30% shorter time-to-data-product?

A8_overlap.R02: C2 and C5 on people cost; C3 and C6 on governed, machine-readable catalog access.
A8_overlap.R04: There is some potential overlap between C5 (TCO) and C4 (Portability), because migration/exit costs are partly reflected in both long-term cost and lock-in
A8_overlap.R06: I would say the C4 and C5, because migration effort and proprietary dependencies can create future costs.

A9_dependence.R02: AI readiness depends on Security (AI capability is only usable if governance permits it); Time-to-Data-Product trades off against Security.
A9_dependence.R04: C3 (AI readiness) and C2 (Time-to-Data-Product) are somewhat dependent: the value of AI readiness is higher when the organization needs to deliver AI/data products rapidly. C4 (Portability) can also become more important when the expected long-term cost or migration impact of a platform is high.
A9_dependence.R06: There are interaction between C4 and C5. Portability becomes more important when the expected long-term cost, pricing uncertainty, or switching exposure of the platform is high. Conversely, lock-in may be less concerning when operating costs are predictable and the platform is expected to remain economically attractive.

B2_missing.R02: Missing: hybrid/multi-platform, i.e. a lakehouse as the core with a warehouse as the serving layer, or Snowflake and Databricks coexisting.
B2_missing.R03: An additional criterion could expertise of the available team or easiness of forming a team with the desired skills
B2_missing.R04: The main missing configuration is a hybrid/multi-platform architecture, where an organization deliberately uses both warehouse and lakehouse technologies, sometimes across multiple cloud providers or environments. This is common in transition states as well as mature enterprises.
B2_missing.R05: I've worked for a project where politics meters.
B2_missing.R06: The main configurations which I saw previously is a hybrid architecture.

C4_missing_context.R02: Regulated scale-up, e.g. healthtech/insurtech: a small data team, high AI ambition and strict PHI/HIPAA rules, where speed and compliance pull against each other.
C4_missing_context.R04: A common missing context is a large enterprise undergoing major cloud/data-platform modernization or migration, where legacy systems, existing investments, interoperability and migration risk strongly influence the architecture decision.
C4_missing_context.R06: Yes. What's missing is the typical big company: tight budget, lots of legacy systems, and no one dominant reason to change.

other_comment.R02: The criteria need operational measurement definitions for managed and serverless platforms, where energy and infrastructure metrics aren't exposed.
other_comment.R06: The framework is clear and covers things architects usually leave unspoken. Its biggest plus is that it looks at long-term impact, not just speed and cost.
